name: Haskell containers
summary: Haskell’s standard package of persistent containers: `Data.Sequence` (finger trees), `Data.Map` and `Data.Set` (weight-balanced trees), `Data.IntMap` (Patricia trees), plus trees and graphs.
intro: The `containers` package ships with GHC and is the default place Haskell programs get maps, sets and sequences. All of its types are immutable, and every stated cost, worst-case or amortized, still holds when versions are shared. `Data.Map` and `Data.Set` are size-balanced binary trees (trees of bounded balance, after Adams 1993 and Nievergelt and Reingold 1973), so lookup, insert and delete take O(log n) and an update copies one path. `Data.IntMap` and `Data.IntSet` use big-endian Patricia trees after Okasaki and Gill, which are especially fast at union and intersection.

`Data.Sequence` is the best-known production finger tree: Hinze and Paterson’s 2-3 finger trees annotated with sizes. It gives O(1) access at both ends, O(log n) concatenation, splitting and indexing, and lazy internals so that `fmap`, `zipWith`, `replicate` and similar functions build results incrementally. Unlike a list, a `Seq` is always finite and strict in its length, and it makes a “rather mediocre” stack: if you only push and pop at one end, a list is faster.

The package grew out of modules first written for other libraries: `Data.Map` carries a 2002 copyright by Daan Leijen and `Data.Sequence` a 2005 one by Ross Paterson. It became a separate package when GHC 6.8.1 split the old `base` library in November 2007. It is actively maintained: 0.8 came out in March 2025 and 0.8.1 on 4 October 2026, and more than 6,000 Hackage packages depend on it directly.
strengths: Ships with GHC and is used by thousands of packages, so it is the common currency for maps, sets and sequences
Every bound holds under persistent use, so keeping and reusing old versions never breaks performance
`Data.Sequence` covers deques, indexing, splitting and concatenation with one type
Strict and lazy variants of maps (`Data.Map.Strict`, `Data.Map.Lazy`) to control thunk build-up
limits: `Seq` is slower than a list for stack-like use and slower than an array for indexing, even when the big-O is the same or better
No hash maps: unordered hashing lives in the separate `unordered-containers` package
A `Seq` must be finite, and its size must not exceed `maxBound :: Int`; going over is not detected

snippet.title: A finger-tree sequence and a weight-balanced map (containers 0.7, GHC 9.10)
source: -- a finger tree: O(1) at both ends, O(log n) split, join and index
-- a weight-balanced tree: insert copies one path, old map stays valid
let prices = Map.fromList [("tea", 3), ("cake", 5)] :: Map.Map String Int

story: `Data.Map` traces back to Daan Leijen’s 2002 implementation of Stephen Adams’s weight-balanced trees, a design from a 1993 functional pearl that keeps a size in every node. `Data.IntMap` followed Okasaki and Gill’s big-endian Patricia trees for integer keys, which merge quickly.

In 2005 Ross Paterson added `Data.Sequence`, based on the 2-3 finger trees that Paterson and Ralf Hinze published in the Journal of Functional Programming in 2006. Their paper notes that the sequence implementation of its section 4.2 is included in GHC and other Haskell implementations. When GHC 6.8.1 split the monolithic `base` library in November 2007, these modules became `containers` 0.1, a new library “split off from base”. GHC still bundles it as a dependency of the compiler itself: GHC 9.10.3 ships containers 0.7.

choices.why: Storing each subtree’s size in its node keeps the tree balanced with simple rules, and the docs give precise bounds for set operations such as union and intersection.
One structure with cheap ends, logarithmic split and concatenation, and size annotations for indexing covers queues, deques and random access lists.
Haskell values are persistent by default, so the package states every cost, worst-case or amortized, as valid even when structures are shared.
Splitting `base` in GHC 6.8.1 let containers be versioned and released on its own while still shipping with the compiler.
